title: The OPTIMAL 6D/WEEK Hypertrophy Program by Mike Israetel Review
summary: NH reviews a free 6-day-a-week upper/lower-style template attributed to Mike Israetel (later revealed not to be his). He finds the skeleton and exercise mix solid but criticises excessive volume, front-loaded junk volume, heavy shoulder/trap/biceps bias, a lower-body skew and missing triceps long head, forearm, neck and upper-back work, and proposes cuts, swaps and an extra rest day.
claims: A good program should run as is without e-books or mesocycle explanations; if it falls apart when the trainee deviates, it is a bad program
Mesocycles, low-volume phases and deloads are unnecessary for hypertrophy; a good program can be run indefinitely
Some influencers make programs complex to look smart; a good program could be scribbled on a restaurant table and still work
Programming a 7-day hypertrophy schedule is hard because more days means more interaction between sessions
Volume and intensity manipulation is the most important part of hypertrophy programming
Bench 6-8 and overhead press 5-8 or 8-10 are good rep ranges for opening compounds
Weighted dips right after heavy bench is junk volume risk; rotate instead: heavy bench with bodyweight dips for volume, or open with weighted dips and follow with bench or push-ups
After two compound presses the chest has room for about one more exercise before it becomes junk volume
Machine crunches lead many to overuse the lower back; prefer stretch-based ab work like leg raises or decline sit-ups
Upper-body days should look like a laundry list of varied exercises
Reorganise exercises freely; if moving one exercise breaks a program, it is a bad program
When adjusting someone else's program, learn the author's biases: Israetel favours volume, so lower his rep ranges (e.g. 8 becomes 4-8 or 6-8)
6x10 leg press after high-bar squats is too much; do 3-4 sets of 8-12
Calves can be trained either low volume, medium intensity, high frequency, or medium-high volume at low frequency; NH prefers high frequency
The template has too much direct shoulder and trap work for a natural; repeating biceps, shoulders and traps on consecutive days is not recoverable
Front-loading volume early in the week is fine unless it turns into junk volume
Use the freed slots for neglected muscles: French press for the triceps long head, finger curls for forearms, neck curls for the neck
The template has too much total volume and is skewed toward lower body, which shows Israetel's own lower-body-dominant bias; reduce lower-body volume
Sumo deficit deadlifts assume you already pull sumo well; a conventional deficit or Romanian deadlift makes more sense
Stiff-leg deadlifts are more strength-oriented accessories; Romanian deadlifts are more hypertrophy-oriented due to more stretch
Supported rows (dumbbell, seal) spare the lower back; keep barbell row reps higher to avoid ego lifting
Pull-ups as fast as possible for 30 reps is pointless; do 4 sets AMRAP at a controlled tempo
Decline sit-ups weighted for 10-15 reps are the best ab exercise for hypertrophy
A lower-body day should be short: a few heavy lifts is enough
Incline close-grip bench is an underrated hybrid of bench and overhead press
AMRAP on the main triceps isolation makes intensity poor; use 8-12 to failure instead
If a 7-day schedule is too much physically or psychologically, add a rest day after day five; it will not kill your gains
Presses are not enough for triceps unless you are gifted; isolate them or end up with spaghetti arms
Calves are a very resilient muscle group that tolerates high volume
The pump is not that important for hypertrophy; occlusion curls as fast as possible are unnecessary
Do hanging knee raises slow and controlled with a stretch at the bottom, not as fast as possible
Compare days by stimulus-to-fatigue ratio: two lower days with the same number of exercises can differ hugely in fatigue
Ending the week with an easy baby day is smart for 7-day programs since day one follows immediately
High volume is junk even if the program only runs five weeks; cutting 20-30% lets you run it continuously
Each day should have about four to six exercises, at least four of them low-fatigue isolations
Upper back is under-trained here; use high frequency for more horizontal rows that do not involve the lower back instead of extra shrugs
Upper-body days should look longer than lower-body days because lower-body exercises move far more tonnage per set
He rates this template one of the two best he has reviewed, alongside Jeff Nippard
